extracted.intended_audience: course coordinators, instructional consultants, and instructors (college mathematics/professional development programs)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and evaluation criteria for running and using classroom visits (observational, student-feedback, peer) to improve college mathematics teaching, including scheduling, data collection, reporting, and giving feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible goals of class visits for instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulleted goals listed on the page: To help instructors develop and articulate teaching goals; To point out positive aspects of instructors’ teaching (give them things to “hang their hats on”); To give instructors an opportunity to voice and discuss their concerns privately; To identify classroom practice areas instructors need to concentrate on for improvement; To expand instructors’ range of teaching strategies; To give inexperienced instructors opportunities to interact with, observe, and receive feedback from more experienced instructors; To encourage instructors to reflect upon and assess their own teaching choices, strategies, and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for trainers
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible goals of class visits for trainers/course coordinators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulleted goals listed on the page: To look for teaching ideas that can be shared with other instructors; To observe each instructor’s approach to implementing teaching techniques covered in the professional development program; To identify particularly strong instructors who would be good candidates for peer visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program structure for visits (semester timeline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended sequencing and use of different types of visits across a semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested structure: Two weeks into semester — course coordinators conduct observational visits; Midway — course coordinators or instructional consultants conduct Student Mid-semester Feedback (or instructors collect their own student feedback); Last third — instructors paired to conduct peer visits. Rationale: begin with early observation to support new instructors/diagnose problems; midterm student feedback allows actionable changes; end with peer visits to develop instructors' ability to assess teaching. Also weigh advantages of each visit type against time/effort; avoid redundant or overly time-consuming programs that reduce receptivity to feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling constraints and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when not to schedule visits and practical timing considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid class periods immediately before exams, right after exams, and near lengthy vacations. Choose days when the instructor will actually be teaching (avoid days with lengthy quizzes/exams). Send a reminder the day before the visit to avoid instructor surprise. For student-feedback sessions, ensure the session is timed so students have enough class experience to give informed opinions but enough time remains to implement changes (mid-semester).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations when working with novice instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles to keep in mind when observing and giving feedback to very new/inexperienced instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key guidelines from the page: (1) Novices often have strongly held beliefs about what 'works' based on their own experiences as students — do not assume a blank slate; ask probing questions when setting up the visit to uncover those beliefs. (2) Novices may be frightened or equate visits with personal evaluation — be sensitive to anxiety. (3) Novices may lack a comprehensive analytic framework for classroom situations and often prefer concrete, straightforward suggestions rather than relativistic analyses. Corollaries/advice: Provide concrete, definite advice (use headings like 'What is going well'); 'catch them doing things right' to build receptivity; be aware that brilliant suggestions may be rejected if incompatible with the instructor's beliefs; do not assume novices are 'blank slates' — probe their prior beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational visits — overall procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Step-by-step procedure for conducting an observational classroom visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps as given: 1) Setting up — contact instructor well in advance, choose an appropriate day, find out instructor goals or aspects they want feedback on, remind day before. 2) The Visit — arrive early, note physical layout and behavior, set up a follow-up meeting time (up to an hour), record as much objective data as possible (avoid value judgments during class). Suggested recording rubrics: draw classroom map, script what is said/done, take lecture notes from student's POV, note significant events. 3) Writing the Report and Planning the Meeting — use notes/maps to compile report under headings (What is going well; Things to watch out for; Suggestions for action); be concrete and specific; value judgments allowed now but grounded in objective data. 4) The Meeting — meet while session is fresh, choose a neutral non-threatening place, thank instructor, begin by asking instructor's goals and what went well, emphasize positives first, corroborate suggestions with objective data, emphasize 2–3 strengths and 2–3 main areas to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation checklist (what to look for)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific items observers should note during the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items adapted from 'Observing Teaching': Note the physical layout of the classroom; How the class begins; Patterns of talk between instructor and students and among students; Patterns of movement; What is written on the blackboard (readability, how long left on board); Types of questions the instructor uses and time to answer; Whether the instructor gives clear directions for activities; Mannerisms of instructor and students (eye contact, tone of voice); How the class ends — is there a summary? Also note student engagement (paying attention, reading newspaper, talking) and specifics of student behavior during activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording methods during observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested recording techniques to gather objective data during the visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested rubrics: draw a classroom map; jot a detailed script of what is said/done; take lecture notes from a student's point of view; note significant events. Avoid value judgments during data collection; collect detailed objective data on both instructor and student behaviors. These methods make subsequent reporting and corroboration more meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report format and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended structure and tone for the written report following an observational visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested headings: 'What is going well in the class', 'Things to watch out for', and 'Suggestions for action.' Be concrete and specific; vague comments confuse instructors. Base value judgments on objective data gathered. Keep reports economical to avoid overwhelming the instructor. Use examples and concrete suggestions that the instructor can act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting etiquette and feedback framing
rubrics_metrics.description: How to conduct the feedback meeting to maximize receptivity and usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet soon while session is fresh; choose a public but non-departmental location (e.g., a coffee shop) to reduce intimidation. Thank the instructor and acknowledge potential stress. Begin with the instructor: ask 'What were your goals for that class session?' and 'What do you think went well?' Insist on discussing positives first (instructors tend to focus on criticisms). Corroborate warnings/suggestions with objective data. Emphasize two or three strengths and two or three main areas for improvement. Check for agreement and clarify communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of constructive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles that make feedback more effective (listed as characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete list from the page: It is descriptive rather than evaluative; It is specific rather than general; It is focused on behavior rather than on the person; It takes into account the needs of both the receiver and giver of feedback; It is directed toward behavior which the receiver can do something about; It is solicited rather than imposed; It is well timed; It involves sharing of information; It involves the amount of information the receiver can use rather than the amount we would like to give; It concerns what is said and done, not how, not why; It is checked to ensure clear communication; It is checked to determine degree of agreement from others; It is followed by attention to the consequences of the feedback; It is an important step toward authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of observational visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits of observational visits for instructors and course coordinators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulleted advantages: Possible very early in semester to support new instructors and diagnose problems; Reports with concrete suggestions give instructors actionable items; Recognition of things done well boosts morale and confidence; Relatively unobtrusive — no class time devoted; Observers who are respected can be influential; Coordinators stay in touch with student body, classroom layouts, and course problems; Feedback can be used to customize and improve overall professional development program and generate distilled handouts of positive instructor qualities or suggested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages and practical limits of observational visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawbacks and logistical/practical challenges of using observational visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulleted disadvantages: Producing accurate, specific, concrete reports is demanding; Reports must be economical to avoid overwhelming instructors — writing fair/informative concise reports requires skill; Many observers may be needed to cover all instructors without overload; Some instructors may interpret visits as evaluations and react strongly; Some instructors may not take observers seriously; Some instructors may view classroom as private between them and students and resist outsiders; Time/effort required may reduce receptivity if program is redundant or overburdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student feedback visits — arranging and instructor pre-brief
rubrics_metrics.description: Items to cover with the instructor before conducting a mid-semester student feedback session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arranging the visit, explain the process and emphasize focusing/moderating the discussion and confidentiality. Cover these five items: Emphasize session will take 20–25 minutes and instructor must leave the room (including collecting papers/answering Qs) with at least 20 minutes left in class; Ask if instructor wants feedback on any specific aspects of the class; Ask instructor to acknowledge your presence or introduce you and the purpose to the class; Set up date/time/place for the follow-up feedback meeting and reserve an hour; Ask if an overhead projector is available (bring two blank transparencies and marker if so). Also confirm not to schedule on test days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student feedback visits — conducting and facilitating the session
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for running the student-feedback group discussion and collecting data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrive early and sit to observe first part of class as in observational visit. Instructor leaves with at least 20 minutes left. Introduce the purpose to the class and form groups of 3–4 (rearrange if they were already working in groups). Ask each group to appoint a recorder and distribute response sheets asking: 'List the major strengths of this course (what is helping you learn?)' and 'List changes that could be made to assist you in learning.' Encourage specificity and practical suggestions. Give 5–7 minutes for group discussion; circulate and monitor; note at least one group listing strengths. If overhead is available, prepare two transparencies labeled 'Strengths' and 'Changes' and record group inputs on them (or have students transcribe to board/handouts if no overhead). Announce when 1–2 minutes remain to keep groups on task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested instructor actions from observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete action suggestions given in example reports to address observed problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: Look for groups not working and encourage cooperation (ask them to explain what they've done or warn they'll be called on); Break long multi-part group activities into checkpoints and discuss intermediate parts to set pace; When someone at the front asks a question, repeat it for all to hear; Enforce higher discipline during quizzes and provide an exercise for early finishers; Move around the room when asking questions to hear more participants; Encourage students sitting out from groups to move and participate; Provide something for students who finish early to work on.
